analysis.one_liner: Requires cosmetics makers to disclose fragrance ingredients and listed harmful chemicals on labels and websites.
analysis.headline: A right-to-know bill for cosmetic ingredient disclosure, introduced with 11 House supporters, was referred to committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that sell cosmetics to list certain fragrance and flavor ingredients — including fragrance allergens and chemicals identified as harmful by the EPA, CDC, and other US, EU, and international health authorities — on the product's packaging and on the company's website. It would also end the practice of treating those ingredient identities as confidential trade secrets, while keeping exact concentrations confidential. Products that fail the disclosure requirements could not legally be sold.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially people with fragrance allergies or chemical sensitivities who currently cannot find out what is in a product's 'fragrance' blend. Salon and beauty workers would gain, too: professional-use products would have to link to a hazard safety data sheet, and the bill defines professional use to cover cosmetology, nail care, barbering, and spa settings.

how_it_helps.text: Within two years, packaging and labels would have to name any ingredient on a long list of chemicals identified as carcinogenic, toxic, or otherwise harmful by the EPA, CDC, and health authorities in California, the EU, Canada, and the WHO, plus EU-listed fragrance allergens above set concentrations; products failing to do so could not be sold.

Within one year, brand owners would have to publish on their websites, in machine-readable and publicly accessible form, any fragrance or flavor ingredient present at 0.01% or above, any listed fragrance allergen, and the ingredient's functional purpose — information that today can be hidden behind the single word 'fragrance'.

The bill would bar treating a required ingredient's identity as a trade secret under federal disclosure law, while leaving its concentration confidential, so companies could not block disclosure of what chemicals they use.
The FDA would have to publish and regularly update a public master list of covered chemicals within six months, notify subscribers of changes, and post semi-annual update summaries.

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics brand owners and fragrance suppliers, who would bear the cost of testing, label redesign, and website disclosure, and would give up the trade-secret protection that has historically kept fragrance formulas private.

drawbacks.text: The covered-chemical list is broad and drawn from sources that are not all hazard lists — for example, it sweeps in every chemical the CDC has detected in human biomonitoring reports — so labels and websites could name many substances with no established harm at the doses in cosmetics, which supporters of the industry argue misleads rather than informs consumers.
Compliance costs fall on every brand that must test formulations and redesign packaging, a burden that weighs heaviest on small and indie cosmetics companies even though the goal is transparency.
Only the ingredient's identity must be disclosed; the concentration stays confidential commercial information, so the transparency is real but partial.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: you would finally be able to see, on the label and online, which allergens and chemicals of concern a product contains, information now hidden behind the word 'fragrance'. The costs are compliance spending by manufacturers and some label clutter from a very broadly drawn chemical list. On balance it is a modest, well-targeted transparency measure rather than a ban; it restricts nothing except secrecy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 8, 2021, joined by Rep. Doris Matsui as an original cosponsor.
Ten additional House Democrats cosponsored the bill, for 11 supporters in total, all Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and three days later to the committee's Health Subcommittee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics brand owners and fragrance suppliers, who keep selling products whose fragrance ingredients remain undisclosed under federal law.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on October 11, 2021, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to take a recorded position against it.

industries.note: The bill would force brands to disclose fragrance ingredients and listed harmful chemicals on labels and websites and would strip trade-secret protection from ingredient identities, at the cost of reformulation testing and packaging changes. Their interest in keeping 'fragrance' formulas secret runs directly against consumers' ability to know what they are putting on their skin.

Suppliers' formulas, marketed to brands under confidentiality, would have to be identified down to the ingredient level on public disclosures. The bill would end the industry-wide practice of hiding individual aroma chemicals behind the generic term 'fragrance'.
